Credit Score Tier Policy — Overview
Credit score tiers determine pricing, required down payment, and manual-underwriting
requirements.

Credit Score Tier Policy — Section 1: Tier Definitions
- 780+: Tier 1 — best available pricing, minimal documentation overlays.
- 740-779: Tier 2 — standard pricing.
- 700-739: Tier 3 — standard pricing with a 0.125% rate add-on.
- 660-699: Tier 4 — requires manual underwriting review for conventional loans.
- 620-659: Tier 5 — FHA/VA only; conventional declined by policy.
- Below 620: Tier 6 — requires exception approval from the Chief Credit Officer; most
 loan types will be declined.

Credit Score Tier Policy — Section 2: Manual Underwriting Triggers
Any credit score below 660 combined with a DTI above 40% requires manual underwriting
regardless of loan type or automated-underwriting-system recommendation.

Document and Data Retention Policy — Overview
This document summarizes retention requirements for mortgage application records and
supporting documentation.

Document and Data Retention Policy — Section 1: Retention Periods
- Approved loan files: retained for 7 years after loan payoff or sale, per investor and
 regulatory requirements.
- Denied application files: retained for 25 months from the date of the adverse-action
 notice, per Regulation B.
- Withdrawn or incomplete applications: retained for 25 months from the date of
 withdrawal or the application deadline, whichever is earlier.

Document and Data Retention Policy — Section 2: Data Access
Only authorized underwriting, compliance, and audit personnel may access unmasked
applicant financial data. All access is logged and reviewed quarterly.

Debt-to-Income (DTI) Ratio Policy — Overview
Debt-to-income ratio (DTI) is the percentage of a borrower's gross monthly income that
goes toward monthly debt payments, including the proposed mortgage payment.

Debt-to-Income (DTI) Ratio Policy — Section 1: Standard Thresholds
- Conventional loans: maximum DTI of 45%, up to 50% with compensating factors
 (reserves >= 6 months, credit score >= 720, or a loan-to-value ratio below 75%).
- FHA loans: maximum DTI of 43%, up to 50% with documented compensating factors.
- VA loans: no hard DTI ceiling, but DTI above 41% requires additional residual-income
 analysis.
- USDA loans: maximum DTI of 41%, front-end ratio capped at 29%.

Debt-to-Income (DTI) Ratio Policy — Section 2: High-Risk Classification
Any application with a DTI at or above 43% is flagged internally as **high-risk** for
portfolio-monitoring purposes, regardless of loan type, and is routed to a senior
underwriter for secondary review.

Debt-to-Income (DTI) Ratio Policy — Section 3: Documentation Requirements
Underwriters must recompute DTI using verified income (paystubs, W-2s, or tax returns for
self-employed borrowers) rather than the applicant-reported figure before final approval.

Denial Reason Definitions — Overview
This document defines the standard denial reason codes used across all origination
channels, aligned to Regulation B adverse-action requirements.

Denial Reason Definitions — Section 1: Definitions
- **Debt-to-income ratio too high**: the borrower's calculated DTI exceeds the maximum
 allowed for the loan program after underwriting review.
- **Credit history**: derogatory items, insufficient credit history, or a credit score
 below the loan program's minimum.
- **Collateral**: the appraised property value is insufficient to support the requested
 loan amount, or the property fails to meet program eligibility standards.
- **Insufficient income**: verified income is insufficient or cannot be reliably
 documented to support the requested payment.
- **Incomplete application**: required documentation was not received within the
 applicable timeframe.
- **Unverifiable information**: information provided by the applicant could not be
 verified through standard channels.
- **Other**: any reason not captured by the above, which must be documented in free text
 by the underwriter.

Denial Reason Definitions — Section 2: Adverse Action Notices
Every denial must generate an adverse-action notice within 30 days of a completed
application, citing the specific denial reason(s) recorded in the system.

High-Risk Application Criteria — Overview
This document defines when an application is classified as high-risk for portfolio
monitoring and secondary review, independent of the final approval decision.

High-Risk Application Criteria — Section 1: High-Risk Triggers
An application is classified as high-risk if **any** of the following is true:
- Debt-to-income ratio is at or above 43%.
- Loan-to-value ratio is at or above 95%.
- Credit score range is below 620.
- The loan is an adjustable-rate product combined with an LTV above 90% (where
 applicable).

High-Risk Application Criteria — Section 2: Handling
High-risk applications require a second underwriter sign-off and are included in the
monthly portfolio-risk report reviewed by the credit committee.

Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio Policy — Overview
Loan-to-value ratio (LTV) is the loan amount divided by the appraised property value (or
purchase price, whichever is lower).

section_title: Section 1: Maximum LTV by Loan Type
text:
Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio Policy — Section 1: Maximum LTV by Loan Type
- Conventional purchase: 97% LTV for first-time buyers, 95% otherwise.
- FHA: 96.5% LTV with a minimum 580 credit score; 90% LTV for scores between 500-579.
- VA: up to 100% LTV for eligible veterans with full entitlement.
- USDA: up to 100% LTV in eligible rural areas.

Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio Policy — Section 2: Private Mortgage Insurance (PMI)
Conventional loans with an LTV above 80% require PMI until the LTV is reduced to 78%
through scheduled amortization, or upon borrower request once at 80%.

Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio Policy — Section 3: High-Risk Classification
Applications with an LTV at or above 95% are flagged as **high-risk** and require
secondary appraisal review, independent of loan type.

State-Specific Lending Overlays — Overview
Certain states impose additional requirements beyond federal and investor guidelines.

State-Specific Lending Overlays — Section 1: Notable State Overlays
- **New York**: requires a state-specific pre-closing disclosure at least 3 business
 days before closing, in addition to federal TRID timing.
- **Texas**: home-equity (Section 50(a)(6)) loans are capped at 80% LTV regardless of
 loan program, and require a 12-day cooling-off period after application.
- **California**: higher-cost mortgage loans are subject to additional disclosure and
 are reviewed by the compliance team before approval.
- **Illinois**: predatory-lending database checks are mandatory for all loans in Cook
 County prior to closing.

State-Specific Lending Overlays — Section 2: Application
State overlays apply based on `property_state`, not the borrower's mailing address, and
are enforced in addition to (never in place of) federal requirements.
